item.title: A Quebec town was once preparing for a big EV battery boost. Will it still come?
item.description: Much of the heavy machinery is at the Nemaska Lithium plant site in Quebec, is at a standstill after majority owner Rio Tinto issued dozens of layoff notices. Workers were not the only thing effected, ...
item.dc:creator: Genevieve Beauchemin
item.content:encoded: BECANCOUR, QUE.- Much of the heavy machinery at the Nemaska Lithium plant site in Quebec, is at a standstill after majority owner Rio Tinto issued dozens of layoff notices. Workers were not the only thing affected, construction on an EV battery chain that was nearly 80 per cent complete is now forced to pause. This marks the latest sign for the town of Bécancour, located in a region known as “Battery Valley,” that plans for the area to become a hub of an EV manufacturing boom may not come to fruition. “Decisions on further investment and project timing at Bécancour will depend on the outcome of the evaluation, project economics, market conditions, and customer needs,” Rio Tinto said in a statement. The global metal and mining giant said it remains confident in the long-term outlook for lithium processing in Quebec and Canada, despite a decline in lithium prices as global demand for battery materials and electric vehicles has slowed. The fallout could hit the town of Bécancour, which is nestled along the shores of the St. Lawrence River halfway between Montreal and Quebec City. The Nemaska plant is vital in Quebec’s plan to set up an EV battery manufacturing chain in the province. In the same plan, the province promised to develop Bécancour into a hub. Slow EV sales halt economic boost As EV batteries and plants started to set up shop in the town’s industrial park in 202, Bécancour estimated it would see a boost of 1,500 direct and 5,000 indirect jobs, including in the restaurant industry and service sector. The population grew slightly with the arrival of workers at construction sites. To accommodate them the city planned to expand schools, build housing and even purchase new ladder trucks for the local fire station. However, when sales of EVs slowed, some projects were paused, while others were completely scrapped. In March, Nemaska announced it would scale down the pace of building its processing plant. Though Quebec owns 46.1 per cent of Nemaska, the province’s new government said this week it would not spend a penny more on the project for the time being. “Our sincere hope is that this is going to work, because I don’t want to be the guy to write off the $1.1 billion we invested,” said Quebec Minister of Economic Development, Innovation and Energy Stéphane Paquet. But many in the Bécancour area say the setbacks are simply bumps in the road that leads to electrification. “The battery file is here to stay,” said the prefect of the region Mario Lyonnais. “I am confident that the Nemaska plant will open. When it does, we will be ready and we will continue to prepare.” Lyonnais says the battery boom was happening very quickly and that it was hard for the municipalities in the region to keep up with the pace of scaling up services. He says the slowdown may allow the area more time to be fully ready for the grand opening of Nemaska and for a time when EV battery manufacturing delivers the region a boost.

item.title: Joly didn't meet with Roshel before deal signed with Stellantis: minister's office
item.description: Industry Minister Mélanie Joly’s office is disputing media reports that characterized the federal government as having played an active role in negotiations that led to automaker Stellantis selling ...
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: Industry Minister Mélanie Joly’s office is disputing media reports that characterized the federal government as having played an active role in negotiations that led to automaker Stellantis selling its Brampton, Ont. assembly plant to defence contractor Roshel. Mathis Denis, a spokesperson for Joly’s office, said Wednesday evening that reporting that Joly “was involved in the deal is false.” “The minister had no part in negotiating with Stellantis or Roshel on the deal,” he said. “The minister was in a conflict resolution (role) between Stellantis and the union. That’s it. The minister didn’t meet Roshel.” Denis said the minister took part in discussions between Stellantis and Unifor, which represents more than 9,000 Canadian workers for the automaker, to find a way forward after the company decided to move production previously earmarked for the Brampton plant to the United States. He said the move, announced in October 2025, was in violation of Stellantis’ commitments to Ottawa tied to a federal commitment of up to $529 million through the Strategic Response Fund (SRF). “Reporting that the minister was involved in the (Roshel) deal is false because the minister, the department and the team would have never approved or agreed to a deal that, first, did not honour their commitment under the SRF, but, second, lacked the union’s approval,” said Denis. “We have already made it clear to Stellantis that if they were going to move forward with a sale or a deal ... that did not honour their commitment under the SRF, we would use the tools at our disposal to respond.” On Tuesday, Prime Minister Mark Carney said that selling the Brampton plant “violates the obligations that Stellantis has under several agreements,” as he called the move “unacceptable.” “But to be more fundamental, it’s a betrayal of the workers as it is a betrayal of the obligations to Canada and by extension to all Canadians,” Carney said. Later that day, CTV News reported — citing three unnamed sources with “direct knowledge” of the talks between Stellantis and Roshel — that Ottawa “was actively and intensively part” of those discussions. The news outlet reported that the federal government engaged “directly” with both companies, knew the terms surrounding the sale and “did not stand in the way of it.” CBC News also reported the federal government was aware for months about the possibility that Stellantis would sell the facility to Roshel and that it was “engaged regularly” since August. Stellantis announced the sale of the facility and associated equipment to Roshel for an undisclosed amount late Monday afternoon. The companies say they expect the transaction to close by the end of this year, however it is subject to certain conditions, including government and regulatory requirements. Roshel CEO Roman Shimonov has said his Brampton-based company is willing to hire back some of the 2,000 Stellantis employees who were laid off from the plant when it halted operations in 2023. The facility had been slated to be retooled for Jeep production, a process that began early in 2024, before Stellantis paused the plan in early 2025. It later announced it was moving production of the Jeep Compass to Illinois, leaving the plant idled indefinitely. Joly is set to convene a meeting Thursday in Toronto with the leadership of Stellantis and Unifor, along with Ontario Economic Development Minister Vic Fedeli. “This is not the outcome we wanted and we have no choice but to find Stellantis in default of their obligation,” said Denis. This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 11, 2026. Sammy Hudes, The Canadian Press With files from Alessia Passafiume in Ottawa

item.title: Market Outlook: Canadian stocks offer exposure to AI buildout
item.description: Lorne Steinberg discusses CoreWeave’s results, software stock valuations and Canadian opportunities tied to AI and infrastructure spending.
item.dc:creator: BNN Bloomberg
item.content:encoded: CoreWeave’s stronger third-quarter results and increased annual guidance have brought renewed attention to the AI cloud sector following a technology sell-off. BNN Bloomberg spoke with Lorne Steinberg, co-president of Lorne Steinberg Wealth Management, about the implications for technology shares and opportunities tied to Canada’s major project buildout. Key Takeaways Read the full transcript below: ROGER: CoreWeave showed a strong third quarter, lifting its guidance for the year. The neocloud provider has been facing pressure in recent months as investors continue to weigh a volatile tech trade. Let’s get more from Lorne Steinberg, co-president of Lorne Steinberg Wealth Management. Lorne, thanks as always for joining us. LORNE: Thank you, Roger. ROGER: OK, it’s been a rough little while, but a good day today for CoreWeave. What do you see they did right, and what’s driving this? LORNE: Well, I think the No. 1 thing is the stock’s been under tremendous pressure, in large part due to the amount of money they’ve had to borrow, and the bond prices for CoreWeave have been decimated, which would have made it very difficult to raise more cash. So today’s print, I think, gives investors, first of all, a lot of comfort that CoreWeave’s revenues are on track. They’ve raised their guidance that they’re going to deliver over $13 billion of revenues this year. Their margins have improved, but I think, really significantly, they’ve indicated, Roger, that they’re only going to have to raise about $5 billion through 2027 to meet their buildout capacity that they have promised to their customers, and they should be easily able to do that at bond prices that would probably be in the seven to eight per cent range. So it’s a huge sigh of relief to investors and takes the pressure off in the near term. ROGER: So, so what does this mean then for other, other neoclouds like Nebulas — Nebius, excuse me — and IREN? LORNE: So, I think a lot of it has to do with the guidance provided that they are massively oversubscribed on the amount of capacity they can build out, so that, to me, makes the whole sector look very stable and strong growth for the next couple of years. I think the biggest issue going forward past, you know, ’27 or ’28 is the — of course, the midterm elections in the States, you know, indicate that we may get fewer data centres built out than are — were originally, you know, on the slate, and that could have a negative impact. The biggest tough thing for CoreWeave, but they’ve shown zero problem with this, is they have to deliver these data centres on time, or else they would be subject to penalties and possibly cancellation. But thus far, there have been — there’s been zero indication of that. So I think the industry is stable for next couple of years. But really, public policy may have some impact on the industry as a whole. But pretty positive for everybody. ROGER: So it’s going to — it sounds like it’s going to take some work. There must — there’s opportunities, though, in these moments, isn’t there? LORNE: Absolutely. The stock is still way down from where it was, but this gives investors a lot of comfort that the company is here to stay for the next few years. That’s for sure. ROGER: All right. Some names that pop up for you within tech: Constellation, Open Text, Adobe, Alphabet. What are you seeing there? What do you see for opportunities there? LORNE: So first of all, let me deal with a couple of Canadian stocks first. So Constellation Software has been a spectacular growth story, growth by acquisition, delivering, you know, 15 per cent annualized revenue growth, which we see continuing going forward. The stock was under pressure and way down from where it was. Of course, because people feared AI would cut into the need for software. But they really deal with small and medium-sized businesses to a great extent. Those companies just don’t have the capacity to do it themselves. So for us, this is — remains a great opportunity to get into one of Canada’s few real growth stories, and a company with a — you know, in a pretty unique position. The second company is Open Text. Open Text has been a zero grower for the past few years. They switched CEOs. We like what’s going on there, but Open Text, Roger, is actually the cheapest company in our portfolio, trading at about six times earnings, delivering significant free cash flow, and the new management team has been very clear that they are there to create value finally for shareholders, and that’s starting to take the form of share — significant share buybacks, as well as investing in growth, but also divesting themselves of assets which were basically going nowhere. On the U.S. side, let me be clear: one of the cheapest stocks we own is Adobe. Adobe, also another software company under pressure because of fears of AI, but there has been absolutely zero indication that anything is being cut out of their business. Every quarter is another 10 per cent-plus revenue and earnings grower, and at 10 times free cash flow, this company is actually buying back significant stock, and, you know, we see the stock worth double the current share price. And, and finally, when we look at Alphabet, you know, just among the best in the world at what they do, the best in many areas. Alphabet’s been under pressure because, of course, the AI spend, the capex they’re putting out, is eating up all of their free cash flow and then some for the next couple of years. That being said, Alphabet has over five — a backlog of over $500 billion. So a lot of this capex will be producing short-term return on investment very quickly. The company’s trading at the cheapest valuation it has in many years, 15 times earnings, and revenues are growing at an astounding 25 per cent, which we expect to continue per year for the next couple of years. So this is just an incredible opportune entry opportunity to get into a company of this quality. ROGER: OK, the other big AI, at least in Canada, the other big story — AI is everywhere, of course — but the big Canadian major project buildout. You’re seeing opportunities there. Finning showing up for you. Toromont, WSP. Some quick reasons on those ones why they’ve got your attention. LORNE: Sure. So Toromont, Toromont and Finning are the largest Caterpillar dealers. Finning’s the largest. Toromont second. And of course, to build out all of these projects, you’re going to need a lot of equipment, and you have nowhere else to go in Canada but Finning and Toromont. So these companies already have a record backlog, and these projects haven’t even started yet. They’ll both benefit from data centre buildout, infrastructure, etc. Interestingly, Toromont also has a division that caters specifically to data centres because they sell power supplies and in — and enclosures for data centres. Canada should be somewhat of a beneficiary if there’s some pushback in the U.S. of — in communities that don’t want to build data centres, and we’re already seeing data centre approvals here in Canada, you know, from the likes of Meta, et cetera. So both these companies are primed to deliver double-digit earnings growth for years to come. They also both happen to be dividend aristocrats, with Finning having raised its dividend every year for 25 straight years, Toromont every year for 37 straight years. So these are just two incredibly fine companies. WSP Global, of course, is the large engineering company, and they are poised to get contracts across the board. Critical minerals as they build out the Ring of Fire, transportation, data centres. The stock has been under pressure with most engineering companies because of fears that AI would require, you know, smaller contracts from large companies. There again is zero evidence of this, and we’re looking at WSP Global to be also a double-digit grower. So here are three Canadian companies that will absolutely benefit from the buildout in Canada. ROGER: All right, we have to wrap it up there, Lorne. But thanks as always for joining us. LORNE: Roger, thank you so much for having me. ROGER: Lorne Steinberg, co-president of Lorne Steinberg Wealth Management. --- This BNN Bloomberg summary and transcript of the Nov. 11, 2026 interview with Lorne Steinberg are published with the assistance of AI.
